questions.title: Exceptions practice 1
questions.prompt: How should standard exceptions usually be caught?
choices: By const reference
By raw pointer
By mutable global value
Only with catch-all
questions.explanation: Catching by const reference avoids copying and preserves the dynamic exception information for the handler.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 2
questions.prompt: What happens to local RAII objects during stack unwinding?
choices: Their destructors run
They are always leaked
They become global
Their constructors run again
questions.explanation: As exception control exits each scope, destructors run for fully constructed local objects and release their resources.

questions.title: Trace Exceptions
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The parser either returns a valid positive count or throws a descriptive exception that the caller handles. The resulting output is 'value must be positive'.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 5
questions.prompt: How does `catch (const std::runtime_error& error)` differ from `catch (...)`?
choices: It catches only runtime_error and can read the error's message with error.what()
It catches every possible exception, the same as catch (...)
It re-throws the exception automatically after the block
It prevents work() from ever throwing
questions.explanation: A typed catch handles one kind of exception and gives you the object, so `error.what()` can report the cause. `catch (...)` catches everything but hands you nothing to inspect, which is why an empty `catch (...)` hides the problem. Neither form stops `work()` from throwing or re-throws on its own.

questions.title: Exception-worthy failure
questions.prompt: When should C++ code use an exception instead of a normal branch?
choices: Use exceptions when a function cannot complete its promised operation.
Catch every exception and continue without evidence.
Use exceptions for ordinary choices an if statement can handle.
Replace the original error with a vague one and drop the cause.
questions.explanation: Ordinary outcomes, such as an empty search result, often belong in normal `if` logic. Exceptions fit failures that prevent a function from doing what it promised, especially when callers need to decide how to recover.

questions.title: Descriptive exception
questions.prompt: What should thrown C++ exceptions communicate?
choices: Throw a vague failure so callers do not see internal details.
Throw a descriptive exception type.
Throw ordinary success states instead of returning normally.
Throw only strings so all exception types look identical.
questions.explanation: An exception should describe the failure clearly enough for a caller or log to understand what went wrong. Vague failures make debugging harder and push context out of the place that knows it.

questions.title: Catch with purpose
questions.prompt: Where should C++ code catch an exception?
choices: At the first possible line, even if that code cannot respond.
In every helper function so failures are always swallowed.
Catch only where recovery or context is possible.
Only at the end of the program after all context is gone.
questions.explanation: Catch an exception where the code can recover, add useful context, or translate the failure for a caller. Catching too early often leaves the program with no real response.

questions.title: Catch by const reference
questions.prompt: How should standard C++ exceptions usually be caught?
choices: Catch standard exceptions by const reference.
Catch standard exceptions by value so derived details are copied away.
Catch standard exceptions as raw pointers.
Catch standard exceptions only with catch-all syntax.
questions.explanation: Catching by `const` reference avoids copying and preserves the real exception type for polymorphic exceptions. Catching by value can slice derived exception details away.

questions.title: Do not silence failures
questions.prompt: Why should a C++ catch block avoid silently ignoring unknown failures?
choices: Do not silence unknown failures.
Keep running after required work did not happen.
Handle errors by returning unrelated default data.
Assume the absence of a crash proves the operation succeeded.
questions.explanation: A silent catch makes required work look successful when it was not. If the layer cannot recover, it should report, add context, or rethrow so the failure is not lost.

questions.title: Failure across calls
questions.prompt: What job do exceptions serve across several function calls?
choices: Use try/catch around code that cannot throw.
Report failures across function calls without losing cleanup.
Make callers guess whether a failure happened.
Discard stack-trace information during wrapping.
questions.explanation: Exceptions can carry failure information to a caller that has enough context to respond. RAII cleanup still runs as the stack unwinds, so resources can be released without manual cleanup at every level.
